Chapter 19 — Ellipse

Kanna, begin with two fixed points and one fixed total distance. The ellipse equation describes that picture.

Your overall target remains 200 marks: Physics 60, Maths 60, Chemistry 80. First learn the axis lengths, foci, eccentricity, directrices and latus rectum. Then connect tangents, normals and maximum/minimum questions to the same picture.

Concept C01 — An ellipse keeps the sum of two distances fixed

Fix two points F1,F2F_1,F_2F1​,F2​, called foci. A moving point PPP belongs to the ellipse when

PF1+PF2=2a.\boxed{PF_1+PF_2=2a}.PF1​+PF2​=2a​.

Here 2a2a2a is a fixed positive length, greater than F1F2F_1F_2F1​F2​. Imagine a loose string with its ends at the foci. Pull it tight with a pencil. The pencil can move, but the two string lengths still add to the same total.

Put the centre halfway between the foci, at O=(0,0)O=(0,0)O=(0,0). Write the foci as (c,0),(−c,0)(c,0),(-c,0)(c,0),(−c,0), where c>0c>0c>0.

The farthest right and left points are (a,0),(−a,0)(a,0),(-a,0)(a,0),(−a,0). Their joining segment is the major axis, length 2a2a2a. Halfway across the top is (0,b)(0,b)(0,b). Its two focal distances are equal, so each is aaa:

c2+b2=a⟹c2=a2−b2.\sqrt{c^2+b^2}=a \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{c^2=a^2-b^2}.c2+b2​=a⟹c2=a2−b2​.

Thus a>b>0a>b>0a>b>0. The minor axis joins (0,b),(0,−b)(0,b),(0,-b)(0,b),(0,−b) and has length 2b2b2b.

The corresponding equation is

x2a2+y2b2=1.\boxed{\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1}.a2x2​+b2y2​=1​.

The curve has −a≤x≤a-a\le x\le a−a≤x≤a and −b≤y≤b-b\le y\le b−b≤y≤b. At x=ax=ax=a, y=0y=0y=0; at x=0x=0x=0, y=±by=\pm by=±b. These quick checks connect the denominators to the actual axis endpoints.

Concept C02 — Read the larger denominator and complete squares first

We use aaa for the semi-major length and bbb for the semi-minor length. So a>b>0a>b>0a>b>0, even when the longer axis is vertical.

Major-axis direction Equation at centre (h,k)(h,k)(h,k) Foci Major-axis ends
horizontal (x−h)2a2+(y−k)2b2=1\dfrac{(x-h)^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{(y-k)^2}{b^2}=1a2(x−h)2​+b2(y−k)2​=1 (h±c,k)(h\pm c,k)(h±c,k) (h±a,k)(h\pm a,k)(h±a,k)
vertical (x−h)2b2+(y−k)2a2=1\dfrac{(x-h)^2}{b^2}+\dfrac{(y-k)^2}{a^2}=1b2(x−h)2​+a2(y−k)2​=1 (h,k±c)(h,k\pm c)(h,k±c) (h,k±a)(h,k\pm a)(h,k±a)

Pattern: the larger denominator is under the coordinate along the longer axis. The coefficient in an unnormalized equation can be misleading.

For example,

4x2+y2=16⟹x24+y216=1.4x^2+y^2=16 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{16}=1.4x2+y2=16⟹4x2​+16y2​=1.

The major axis is vertical: a=4,b=2a=4,b=2a=4,b=2, not the reverse.

For a general axis-aligned quadratic, group the xxx and yyy terms, complete both squares and then divide to make the right side 1. Check that both squared denominators are positive; otherwise the equation may not describe a real ellipse.

The filled area is

A=πab.\boxed{A=\pi ab}.A=πab​.

One way to see it: a unit disc has area π\piπ. Stretch horizontal distances by aaa and vertical distances by bbb. Every small area is multiplied by ababab. This gives an ellipse, though this unequal stretch does not preserve angles.

Concept C03 — Eccentricity and directrices

Eccentricity compares the centre-to-focus distance with the semi-major length:

e=ca=1−b2a2.\boxed{e=\frac ca=\sqrt{1-\frac{b^2}{a^2}}}.e=ac​=1−a2b2​​​.

For a noncircular ellipse, 0<e<10<e<10<e<1. The foci lie inside the major-axis ends because c<ac<ac<a. If bbb gets close to aaa, eee gets close to 0 and the ellipse gets close to a circle. If b/ab/ab/a becomes small, eee gets close to 1 and the ellipse becomes long and narrow.

A horizontal ellipse also obeys the focus–directrix rule:

PF=e PD,\boxed{PF=e\,PD},PF=ePD​,

where DDD is the perpendicular foot on the corresponding directrix. For focus (c,0)(c,0)(c,0), that line is x=a/ex=a/ex=a/e; for focus (−c,0)(-c,0)(−c,0), it is x=−a/ex=-a/ex=−a/e.

At centre (h,k)(h,k)(h,k), horizontal directrices are x=h±a/ex=h\pm a/ex=h±a/e; vertical directrices are y=k±a/ey=k\pm a/ey=k±a/e. The distance between the directrices is 2a/e2a/e2a/e, while the distance between foci is 2ae2ae2ae. They are different lengths.

Important for JEE Main: match a focus with its corresponding directrix. The focus and centre are different points. Do not use the focus as the centre of a circle.

For a circle, e=0e=0e=0 and both foci merge at the centre. The finite-directrix formulas containing 1/e1/e1/e do not apply at e=0e=0e=0.

Concept C04 — Focal distances and the full latus rectum

For the horizontal ellipse and right focus F1=(c,0)F_1=(c,0)F1​=(c,0),

PF1=a−ex,PF2=a+ex,F2=(−c,0).\boxed{PF_1=a-ex},\qquad \boxed{PF_2=a+ex},\quad F_2=(-c,0).PF1​=a−ex​,PF2​=a+ex​,F2​=(−c,0).

Why are they so short? Their sum is 2a2a2a. Their squared difference is

PF22−PF12=(x+c)2−(x−c)2=4cx.PF_2^2-PF_1^2=(x+c)^2-(x-c)^2=4cx.PF22​−PF12​=(x+c)2−(x−c)2=4cx.

Factor the left side as (PF2−PF1)(PF2+PF1)(PF_2-PF_1)(PF_2+PF_1)(PF2​−PF1​)(PF2​+PF1​). Since the sum is 2a2a2a, their difference is 2cx/a=2ex2cx/a=2ex2cx/a=2ex. Adding/subtracting the sum and difference gives the two formulas.

Both are positive. The smallest distance to a fixed focus is a−c=a(1−e)a-c=a(1-e)a−c=a(1−e), reached at the near major-axis end. The largest is a+c=a(1+e)a+c=a(1+e)a+c=a(1+e), reached at the opposite end.

A focal chord has two curve endpoints and passes through a focus. The latus rectum is the focal chord perpendicular to the major axis.

For the right focus, put x=c=aex=c=aex=c=ae:

c2a2+y2b2=1⟹y=±b2a.\frac{c^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=\pm\frac{b^2}{a}.a2c2​+b2y2​=1⟹y=±ab2​.

Therefore

endpoints=(c,±b2a),full latus-rectum length=2b2a.\boxed{\text{endpoints}=\left(c,\pm\frac{b^2}{a}\right)},\qquad \boxed{\text{full latus-rectum length}=\frac{2b^2}{a}}.endpoints=(c,±ab2​)​,full latus-rectum length=a2b2​​.

Important for JEE Main: b2/ab^2/ab2/a is a half chord length. 2b2b2b is the full minor-axis length. Many wrong options mix these with the full latus rectum.

Concept C05 — The eccentric angle labels a point

For a horizontal ellipse,

P=(acos⁡θ,bsin⁡θ).\boxed{P=(a\cos\theta,b\sin\theta)}.P=(acosθ,bsinθ)​.

Substitution gives cos⁡2θ+sin⁡2θ=1\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1cos2θ+sin2θ=1, so this always lies on the ellipse. As θ\thetaθ runs through one full turn, it covers the whole curve.

Why call it an eccentric angle? Draw the auxiliary circle of radius aaa. On that circle take U=(acos⁡θ,asin⁡θ)U=(a\cos\theta,a\sin\theta)U=(acosθ,asinθ). Keep its xxx-coordinate and shorten its height by the ratio b/ab/ab/a. This produces PPP.

The angle θ\thetaθ belongs to OUOUOU. It is generally not the angle made by OPOPOP with the xxx-axis. If that polar angle is ϕ\phiϕ, then, when the ratios are defined,

tan⁡ϕ=batan⁡θ.\tan\phi=\frac{b}{a}\tan\theta.tanϕ=ab​tanθ.

For a vertical ellipse use (bcos⁡θ,asin⁡θ)(b\cos\theta,a\sin\theta)(bcosθ,asinθ). For a shifted ellipse add its centre coordinates.

Use the parameter when the question gives an angle, asks for a moving tangent, or contains products of ellipse coordinates. The familiar identity sin⁡2θ+cos⁡2θ=1\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1sin2θ+cos2θ=1 often replaces a longer elimination.

Concept C06 — Tangent: the curve's direction at one point

A tangent follows the curve's local direction at the touching point. At a curve point (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​), differentiating gives

2xa2+2yb2y′=0⟹y′=−b2xa2y(y≠0).\frac{2x}{a^2}+\frac{2y}{b^2}y'=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y'=-\frac{b^2x}{a^2y}\quad(y\ne0).a22x​+b22y​y′=0⟹y′=−a2yb2x​(y=0).

Using this slope and the curve equation gives

xx1a2+yy1b2=1.\boxed{\frac{xx_1}{a^2}+\frac{yy_1}{b^2}=1}.a2xx1​​+b2yy1​​=1​.

This point formula also works at the axis ends, where the divided slope formula may fail. At (a,0)(a,0)(a,0) the tangent is x=ax=ax=a; at (0,b)(0,b)(0,b) it is y=by=by=b.

At parameter θ\thetaθ,

xcos⁡θa+ysin⁡θb=1.\boxed{\frac{x\cos\theta}{a}+\frac{y\sin\theta}{b}=1}.axcosθ​+bysinθ​=1​.

For a finite slope mmm, write the line as y=mx+c0y=mx+c_0y=mx+c0​. Its tangency condition is

c02=a2m2+b2.\boxed{c_0^2=a^2m^2+b^2}.c02​=a2m2+b2​.

There are two parallel tangents with intercepts ±a2m2+b2\pm\sqrt{a^2m^2+b^2}±a2m2+b2​. This family also includes horizontal tangents, m=0m=0m=0; vertical ones need x=±ax=\pm ax=±a separately.

For a proper line Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0Ax+By+C=0, the coordinate-independent coefficient test is

C2=a2A2+b2B2.\boxed{C^2=a^2A^2+b^2B^2}.C2=a2A2+b2B2​.

You can derive it by substituting the line into the ellipse and requiring a repeated intersection. It includes vertical and horizontal lines.

Check first: a formula for a tangent at a point requires that point to be on the ellipse. An external point instead gives two contacts, as in C10.

Concept C07 — Normal: a line perpendicular to the tangent

At P=(x1,y1)P=(x_1,y_1)P=(x1​,y1​), a normal points in direction

(x1a2,y1b2).\boxed{\left(\frac{x_1}{a^2},\frac{y_1}{b^2}\right)}.(a2x1​​,b2y1​​)​.

Why? The tangent equation has those two coefficients. They give a perpendicular direction, just as for a straight line Ax+By=CAx+By=CAx+By=C. The normal passes through PPP:

(x,y)=(x1,y1)+t(x1a2,y1b2).(x,y)=(x_1,y_1)+t\left(\frac{x_1}{a^2},\frac{y_1}{b^2}\right).(x,y)=(x1​,y1​)+t(a2x1​​,b2y1​​).

When x1y1≠0x_1y_1\ne0x1​y1​=0, an equivalent useful form is

a2xx1−b2yy1=a2−b2.\boxed{\frac{a^2x}{x_1}-\frac{b^2y}{y_1}=a^2-b^2}.x1​a2x​−y1​b2y​=a2−b2​.

The normal slope is a2y1/(b2x1)a^2y_1/(b^2x_1)a2y1​/(b2x1​) when x1≠0x_1\ne0x1​=0. At a major-axis end the normal is the major axis. At a minor-axis end it is the minor axis.

Important distinction: an ellipse's normal does not usually pass through its centre. A radius-to-contact direction is automatically normal for a circle, but not for a general ellipse. Here the normal direction is (x1/a2,y1/b2)(x_1/a^2,y_1/b^2)(x1​/a2,y1​/b2), rather than (x1,y1)(x_1,y_1)(x1​,y1​).

Concept C08 — Perpendicular distances from the foci to a tangent

This question is about two shortest segments from fixed foci to a line. It is different from the two segments joining a curve point to its foci.

For any tangent,

d1d2=b2,\boxed{d_1d_2=b^2},d1​d2​=b2​,

where d1,d2d_1,d_2d1​,d2​ are the perpendicular distances from the two foci.

Here is a short reason. A unit normal is a perpendicular direction arrow of length 1. Write the tangent as nxx+nyy=hn_xx+n_yy=hnx​x+ny​y=h, choosing that unit normal, so nx2+ny2=1n_x^2+n_y^2=1nx2​+ny2​=1 and h>0h>0h>0. From C06,

h2=a2nx2+b2ny2.h^2=a^2n_x^2+b^2n_y^2.h2=a2nx2​+b2ny2​.

The foci are (±c,0)(\pm c,0)(±c,0) and lie on the centre's side of the tangent, so their distances are h−cnxh-cn_xh−cnx​ and h+cnxh+cn_xh+cnx​. Multiply:

d1d2=h2−c2nx2=(a2−c2)nx2+b2ny2=b2(nx2+ny2)=b2.\begin{aligned} d_1d_2&=h^2-c^2n_x^2\\ &=(a^2-c^2)n_x^2+b^2n_y^2\\ &=b^2(n_x^2+n_y^2)=b^2. \end{aligned}d1​d2​​=h2−c2nx2​=(a2−c2)nx2​+b2ny2​=b2(nx2​+ny2​)=b2.​

No angle needs to be calculated. Use this when the wording specifically says perpendicular distances to a tangent.

Concept C09 — Chord with a given midpoint

Let M=(h,k)M=(h,k)M=(h,k) be the midpoint and let endpoints be (h+u,k+v),(h−u,k−v)(h+u,k+v),(h-u,k-v)(h+u,k+v),(h−u,k−v). Substitute both in the ellipse and subtract. The matching squares cancel:

hua2+kvb2=0.\frac{hu}{a^2}+\frac{kv}{b^2}=0.a2hu​+b2kv​=0.

So the direction (u,v)(u,v)(u,v) is perpendicular to (h/a2,k/b2)(h/a^2,k/b^2)(h/a2,k/b2). The chord line is

hxa2+kyb2=h2a2+k2b2.\boxed{\frac{hx}{a^2}+\frac{ky}{b^2} =\frac{h^2}{a^2}+\frac{k^2}{b^2}}.a2hx​+b2ky​=a2h2​+b2k2​​.

For a noncentral midpoint, a real nonzero chord needs

h2a2+k2b2<1.\frac{h^2}{a^2}+\frac{k^2}{b^2}<1.a2h2​+b2k2​<1.

Equality gives a collapsed chord on the boundary; a value greater than 1 gives no such real chord. If M=(0,0)M=(0,0)M=(0,0), every diameter has that midpoint, so there is no unique chord and the displayed equation reduces to 0=00=00=0.

Pattern to remember: a midpoint formula has the midpoint's own quadratic value on the right. Replacing it by 1 would wrongly treat the midpoint as a tangent contact.

Concept C10 — Chord of contact from an external point

From an external point Q=(x0,y0)Q=(x_0,y_0)Q=(x0​,y0​), draw two tangents touching at A,BA,BA,B. The segment ABABAB is the chord of contact.

The tangent at A=(x1,y1)A=(x_1,y_1)A=(x1​,y1​) passes through QQQ, so

x0x1a2+y0y1b2=1.\frac{x_0x_1}{a^2}+\frac{y_0y_1}{b^2}=1.a2x0​x1​​+b2y0​y1​​=1.

The second contact obeys the same equation. Therefore their common line is

x0xa2+y0yb2=1.\boxed{\frac{x_0x}{a^2}+\frac{y_0y}{b^2}=1}.a2x0​x​+b2y0​y​=1​.

The same-looking expression means different things depending on the role of (x0,y0)(x_0,y_0)(x0​,y0​):

Position of the given point Meaning
x02/a2+y02/b2=1x_0^2/a^2+y_0^2/b^2=1x02​/a2+y02​/b2=1 one tangent at that point
x02/a2+y02/b2>1x_0^2/a^2+y_0^2/b^2>1x02​/a2+y02​/b2>1 two real tangents; their contact chord
x02/a2+y02/b2<1x_0^2/a^2+y_0^2/b^2<1x02​/a2+y02​/b2<1 inside; no real tangents from it

Do not confuse this contact chord with the chord having (x0,y0)(x_0,y_0)(x0​,y0​) as its midpoint.

Concept C11 — Perpendicular tangents and the director circle

A director circle is the locus of the intersection point of two perpendicular tangents.

Take Q=(x0,y0)Q=(x_0,y_0)Q=(x0​,y0​). A finite-slope tangent through it has intercept c0=y0−mx0c_0=y_0-mx_0c0​=y0​−mx0​. Put this into C06:

(y0−mx0)2=a2m2+b2,(y_0-mx_0)^2=a^2m^2+b^2,(y0​−mx0​)2=a2m2+b2,

or

(x02−a2)m2−2x0y0m+(y02−b2)=0.(x_0^2-a^2)m^2-2x_0y_0m+(y_0^2-b^2)=0.(x02​−a2)m2−2x0​y0​m+(y02​−b2)=0.

For two finite slopes to be perpendicular their product must be −1-1−1:

y02−b2x02−a2=−1⟹x02+y02=a2+b2.\frac{y_0^2-b^2}{x_0^2-a^2}=-1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{x_0^2+y_0^2=a^2+b^2}.x02​−a2y02​−b2​=−1⟹x02​+y02​=a2+b2​.

The vertical/horizontal pairs are included too: at (±a,±b)(\pm a,\pm b)(±a,±b), tangents x=±ax=\pm ax=±a and y=±by=\pm by=±b meet at 90∘90^\circ90∘. These points complete the cases omitted by dividing by x02−a2x_0^2-a^2x02​−a2.

This circle has centre at the ellipse's centre and radius a2+b2\sqrt{a^2+b^2}a2+b2​. It is not the ellipse itself.

Concept C12 — Maximum/minimum: use the ellipse's own constraint

For a first-quadrant point (x,y)(x,y)(x,y), define

X=xa,Y=yb.X=\frac xa,\qquad Y=\frac yb.X=ax​,Y=by​.

Then X2+Y2=1X^2+Y^2=1X2+Y2=1, with X,Y≥0X,Y\ge0X,Y≥0.

Important for JEE Main — AM–GM and Cauchy–Schwarz. They turn this constraint into a useful bound:

(X−Y)2≥0⟹2XY≤X2+Y2=1.(X-Y)^2\ge0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2XY\le X^2+Y^2=1.(X−Y)2≥0⟹2XY≤X2+Y2=1.

Equivalently, AM–GM on X2,Y2X^2,Y^2X2,Y2 gives XY≤1/2XY\le1/2XY≤1/2. Equality requires X=Y=1/2X=Y=1/\sqrt2X=Y=1/2​.

Cauchy–Schwarz says the square of a dot product cannot exceed the product of squared lengths:

(uX+vY)2≤(u2+v2)(X2+Y2).(uX+vY)^2\le(u^2+v^2)(X^2+Y^2).(uX+vY)2≤(u2+v2)(X2+Y2).

Here all symbols are real. For example, (X+Y)2≤2(X+Y)^2\le2(X+Y)2≤2, with equality at X=YX=YX=Y. For a linear target on the ellipse,

∣px+qy∣≤a2p2+b2q2.\boxed{|px+qy|\le\sqrt{a^2p^2+b^2q^2}}.∣px+qy∣≤a2p2+b2q2​​.

This follows by using the two pairs (ap,bq)(ap,bq)(ap,bq) and (X,Y)(X,Y)(X,Y). Equality means those pairs point in the same or opposite direction. This helps with largest/smallest linear expressions and tangent support lines.

Largest rectangle parallel to the axes: its four vertices are (±x,±y)(\pm x,\pm y)(±x,±y), so

AR=4xy=4abXY≤2ab.A_R=4xy=4abXY\le\boxed{2ab}.AR​=4xy=4abXY≤2ab​.

Smallest intercept triangle from a tangent: at (acos⁡θ,bsin⁡θ)(a\cos\theta,b\sin\theta)(acosθ,bsinθ) its finite intercepts are

A=(acos⁡θ,0),B=(0,bsin⁡θ).A=\left(\frac a{\cos\theta},0\right),\qquad B=\left(0,\frac b{\sin\theta}\right).A=(cosθa​,0),B=(0,sinθb​).

Ordinary area is positive, so

AT=ab2∣sin⁡θcos⁡θ∣=ab∣sin⁡2θ∣≥ab.A_T=\frac{ab}{2|\sin\theta\cos\theta|} =\frac{ab}{|\sin2\theta|}\ge\boxed{ab}.AT​=2∣sinθcosθ∣ab​=∣sin2θ∣ab​≥ab​.

Equality needs ∣sin⁡2θ∣=1|\sin2\theta|=1∣sin2θ∣=1. Exclude sin⁡θ=0\sin\theta=0sinθ=0 or cos⁡θ=0\cos\theta=0cosθ=0: those tangents do not give a finite two-intercept triangle.

Notice how the same normalized-coordinate product gives a maximum for the rectangle and a minimum for its reciprocal in the triangle problem. Decide what quantity is actually being optimized.

Concept C13 — Build an ellipse from a locus condition

A locus is the set of all points satisfying the stated condition.

For two foci separated by 2c2c2c:

  • a fixed distance sum 2a>2c2a>2c2a>2c gives a nondegenerate ellipse;
  • sum 2c2c2c gives the focal line segment, not a genuine ellipse;
  • sum smaller than 2c2c2c gives no point, by the triangle inequality.

For a focus and a line, start with

(x−fx)2+(y−fy)2=e ∣Ax+By+C∣A2+B2,0<e<1.\sqrt{(x-f_x)^2+(y-f_y)^2} =e\,\frac{|Ax+By+C|}{\sqrt{A^2+B^2}}, \quad 0<e<1.(x−fx​)2+(y−fy​)2​=eA2+B2​∣Ax+By+C∣​,0<e<1.

The focus must be off the directrix and the line must be proper. Both sides are nonnegative, so squaring is safe. Complete squares to find the centre and axis lengths. Check a point in the original distance rule afterward.

Useful order: identify the axis from the foci; find aaa from a distance sum or c/ec/ec/e; then find b2=a2−c2b^2=a^2-c^2b2=a2−c2. Guessing an equation from only one focus loses needed information.

Recall habit: find the centre and the two axis lengths first. Then name the object: focus, tangent point, normal point, midpoint or external point. Similar-looking formulas can describe different objects.

Worked solutions to the 25 PDF questions

Read the question first. Notice the pattern, choose a route, then calculate. Alternative methods below are fully visible.

Question 1 — Eccentricity measures the focal separation compared with the major axis

PDF page 97 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C03

The eccentricity of the ellipse x225+y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=125x2​+16y2​=1 is

  • (a) 45\dfrac4554​
  • (b) 34\dfrac3443​
  • (c) 35\dfrac3553​
  • (d) 925\dfrac9{25}259​

First read the two lengths. The larger denominator is 25, so the major axis is horizontal:

a=5,b=4.a=5,\qquad b=4.a=5,b=4.

The focus is ccc units from the centre, with c2=a2−b2c^2=a^2-b^2c2=a2−b2:

c2=25−16=9,c=3.c^2=25-16=9,\qquad c=3.c2=25−16=9,c=3.

Eccentricity is a ratio of those lengths:

e=ca=35;(c).\boxed{e=\frac ca=\frac35;\quad\text{(c)}}.e=ac​=53​;(c)​.

Check: it must lie between 0 and 1. The value 9/259/259/25 is e2e^2e2, not eee.

Question 2 — Normalize the equation before reading the axis lengths

PDF page 97 | MCQ | Notes: C02,C04

The length of the latus rectum of the ellipse 9x2+16y2=1449x^2+16y^2=1449x2+16y2=144 is

  • (a) 92\dfrac9229​
  • (b) 94\dfrac9449​
  • (c) 323\dfrac{32}3332​
  • (d) 666

Normalize first. The coefficients 9 and 16 are not the squared semiaxes. Divide the whole equation by 144:

x216+y29=1.\frac{x^2}{16}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1.16x2​+9y2​=1.

Thus a=4,b=3a=4,b=3a=4,b=3. The latus rectum is the full chord through a focus perpendicular to the major axis:

L=2b2a=2(9)4=92;(a).\boxed{L=\frac{2b^2}{a}=\frac{2(9)}4=\frac92;\quad\text{(a)}}.L=a2b2​=42(9)​=29​;(a)​.

Coordinate check: c=7c=\sqrt7c=7​. At x=7x=\sqrt7x=7​, the equation gives y=±9/4y=\pm9/4y=±9/4. Their separation is 9/4−(−9/4)=9/29/4-(-9/4)=9/29/4−(−9/4)=9/2.

Question 3 — The foci fix the axis and the given point fixes the minor end

PDF page 97 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C02

The equation of the ellipse with foci at (±3,0)(\pm3,0)(±3,0) and passing through the point (0,4)(0,4)(0,4) is

  • (a) x216+y225=1\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{25}=116x2​+25y2​=1
  • (b) x225+y29=1\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=125x2​+9y2​=1
  • (c) x29+y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=19x2​+16y2​=1
  • (d) x225+y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=125x2​+16y2​=1

Use the distance-sum meaning. At the given point P=(0,4)P=(0,4)P=(0,4), both focus distances are

32+42=5.\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5.32+42​=5.

So PF1+PF2=10=2aPF_1+PF_2=10=2aPF1​+PF2​=10=2a, giving a=5a=5a=5. The foci are 3 units from the origin, so c=3c=3c=3.

b2=a2−c2=25−9=16.b^2=a^2-c^2=25-9=16.b2=a2−c2=25−9=16.

The foci are horizontal, so the equation is

x225+y216=1;(d).\boxed{\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{16}=1;\quad\text{(d)}}.25x2​+16y2​=1;(d)​.

Another possible approach: symmetry makes (0,4)(0,4)(0,4) the upper minor-axis end, so b=4b=4b=4. Then a2=b2+c2=16+9=25a^2=b^2+c^2=16+9=25a2=b2+c2=16+9=25 directly. Both routes work; the focal-sum route also explains why this is an ellipse.

Check: substituting (0,4)(0,4)(0,4) gives 1, and its foci are (±25−16,0)=(±3,0)(\pm\sqrt{25-16},0)=(\pm3,0)(±25−16​,0)=(±3,0).

Question 4 — Translate the two named lengths into formulas

PDF page 97 | MCQ | Notes: C03,C04

If the length of the latus rectum of an ellipse is half of its minor axis, its eccentricity is

  • (a) 12\dfrac1221​
  • (b) 12\dfrac1{\sqrt2}2​1​
  • (c) 32\dfrac{\sqrt3}223​​
  • (d) 34\dfrac{\sqrt3}443​​

Name both lengths before comparing. The full minor axis is 2b2b2b. Half of it is bbb. The full latus rectum is 2b2/a2b^2/a2b2/a.

2b2a=b.\frac{2b^2}{a}=b.a2b2​=b.

Since b>0b>0b>0, divide by bbb:

ba=12.\frac ba=\frac12.ab​=21​.

Now

e2=1−b2a2=1−14=34,e=32;(c).e^2=1-\frac{b^2}{a^2}=1-\frac14=\frac34, \qquad \boxed{e=\frac{\sqrt3}{2};\quad\text{(c)}}.e2=1−a2b2​=1−41​=43​,e=23​​;(c)​.

Check: only the ratio b/ab/ab/a is fixed. There is no need to invent numerical axis lengths. The diagram's a=4,b=2a=4,b=2a=4,b=2 is one example with that ratio.

Question 5 — A fixed tangent slope determines the intercept size

PDF page 97 | Numerical value | Notes: C06

If the line y=x+cy=x+cy=x+c is tangent to the ellipse x29+y24=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}=19x2​+4y2​=1, then c2=c^2=c2= ____.

The slope is known: m=1m=1m=1. For the source ellipse, a2=9,b2=4a^2=9,b^2=4a2=9,b2=4. A tangent y=mx+cy=mx+cy=mx+c must satisfy

c2=a2m2+b2.c^2=a^2m^2+b^2.c2=a2m2+b2.

Therefore

c2=9(1)2+4=13.\boxed{c^2=9(1)^2+4=13}.c2=9(1)2+4=13​.

There are two possible intercepts, c=±13c=\pm\sqrt{13}c=±13​, but the requested square is the same.

Another possible approach — repeated intersection: substitute y=x+cy=x+cy=x+c:

4x2+9(x+c)2=36⟹13x2+18cx+9c2−36=0.4x^2+9(x+c)^2=36 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 13x^2+18cx+9c^2-36=0.4x2+9(x+c)2=36⟹13x2+18cx+9c2−36=0.

For tangency its discriminant is zero:

324c2−52(9c2−36)=0⟹144(13−c2)=0.324c^2-52(9c^2-36)=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 144(13-c^2)=0.324c2−52(9c2−36)=0⟹144(13−c2)=0.

This gives the same c2=13c^2=13c2=13 and shows why a repeated root is the correct condition.

Question 6 — The sum of focal distances is the major-axis length

PDF page 97 | MCQ | Notes: C01

For any point PPP on the ellipse 4x2+9y2=364x^2+9y^2=364x2+9y2=36, the sum of its distances from the two foci is

  • (a) 333
  • (b) 999
  • (c) 121212
  • (d) 666

The question asks for a sum of focal distances. That is the definition PF1+PF2=2aPF_1+PF_2=2aPF1​+PF2​=2a.

Normalize:

4x2+9y2=36⟹x29+y24=1.4x^2+9y^2=36 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{4}=1.4x2+9y2=36⟹9x2​+4y2​=1.

Here a=3a=3a=3, so

PF1+PF2=6;(d).\boxed{PF_1+PF_2=6;\quad\text{(d)}}.PF1​+PF2​=6;(d)​.

Check at a simple point: P=(0,2)P=(0,2)P=(0,2) and foci (±5,0)(\pm\sqrt5,0)(±5​,0) give each distance 5+4=3\sqrt{5+4}=35+4​=3. Finding a general moving point would create work that the fixed-sum definition already avoids.

Question 7 — Minimize an actual finite intercept triangle

PDF page 97 | Numerical value | Notes: C05,C12

A tangent at a variable point of the ellipse x216+y29=1\dfrac{x^2}{16}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=116x2​+9y2​=1 meets the coordinate axes at AAA and BBB. The minimum area of triangle OABOABOAB (OOO the origin) is ____.

First draw what the area belongs to. It is triangle OABOABOAB, formed by the axes and a tangent. It is not an area inside the ellipse.

Take its contact as P=(4cos⁡θ,3sin⁡θ)P=(4\cos\theta,3\sin\theta)P=(4cosθ,3sinθ). The tangent is

xcos⁡θ4+ysin⁡θ3=1.\frac{x\cos\theta}{4}+\frac{y\sin\theta}{3}=1.4xcosθ​+3ysinθ​=1.

Putting y=0y=0y=0 and x=0x=0x=0 gives intercepts 4/cos⁡θ4/\cos\theta4/cosθ and 3/sin⁡θ3/\sin\theta3/sinθ.

Use the absolute value because ordinary area is positive in every quadrant:

Δ=12∣4cos⁡θ3sin⁡θ∣=12∣sin⁡2θ∣≥12.\Delta=\frac12\left|\frac4{\cos\theta}\frac3{\sin\theta}\right| =\frac{12}{|\sin2\theta|}\ge12.Δ=21​​cosθ4​sinθ3​​=∣sin2θ∣12​≥12.

Equality is possible at θ=π/4\theta=\pi/4θ=π/4, giving

P=(22,32),A=(42,0),B=(0,32).P=\left(2\sqrt2,\frac3{\sqrt2}\right),\quad A=(4\sqrt2,0),\quad B=(0,3\sqrt2).P=(22​,2​3​),A=(42​,0),B=(0,32​).

Thus

Δmin⁡=12.\boxed{\Delta_{\min}=12}.Δmin​=12​.

Another possible approach — AM–GM on the intercepts: write the tangent as x/p+y/q=1x/p+y/q=1x/p+y/q=1, with finite nonzero p,qp,qp,q. Its tangency condition is

16p2+9q2=1.\frac{16}{p^2}+\frac9{q^2}=1.p216​+q29​=1.

AM–GM gives 1≥2144/(p2q2)=24/∣pq∣1\ge2\sqrt{144/(p^2q^2)}=24/|pq|1≥2144/(p2q2)​=24/∣pq∣, so ∣pq∣/2≥12|pq|/2\ge12∣pq∣/2≥12. Equality gives ∣p∣=42,∣q∣=32|p|=4\sqrt2,|q|=3\sqrt2∣p∣=42​,∣q∣=32​.

The parameter route is easier to picture. The intercept route is useful if the question already gives intercepts. Axis-end tangents have a missing/infinite intercept and do not make a finite triangle; they cannot be used to claim area zero.

Question 8 — Focal half-separation and eccentricity give the semi-major axis

PDF page 97 | Numerical value | Notes: C02,C03

An ellipse has foci (±3,0)(\pm3,0)(±3,0) and eccentricity 35\dfrac3553​. If its area is kπk\pikπ, then k=k=k= ____.

The given focal coordinate is ccc, not aaa. From foci (±3,0)(\pm3,0)(±3,0), c=3c=3c=3. Since e=c/a=3/5e=c/a=3/5e=c/a=3/5,

a=ce=33/5=5.a=\frac ce=\frac3{3/5}=5.a=ec​=3/53​=5.

Then

b2=a2−c2=25−9=16,b=4.b^2=a^2-c^2=25-9=16,\qquad b=4.b2=a2−c2=25−9=16,b=4. A=πab=20π⟹k=20.A=\pi ab=20\pi \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{k=20}.A=πab=20π⟹k=20​.

Check: c/a=3/5c/a=3/5c/a=3/5 and a2−b2=9a^2-b^2=9a2−b2=9 reproduce both givens.

Question 9 — A fixed sum of distances is an ellipse definition

PDF page 97 | MCQ | Notes: C01,C13

The locus of a point PPP such that the sum of its distances from (4,0)(4,0)(4,0) and (−4,0)(-4,0)(−4,0) is 101010 is

  • (a) x225+y216=1\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{16}=125x2​+16y2​=1
  • (b) x225+y29=1\dfrac{x^2}{25}+\dfrac{y^2}{9}=125x2​+9y2​=1
  • (c) x29+y225=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{25}=19x2​+25y2​=1
  • (d) x2100+y236=1\dfrac{x^2}{100}+\dfrac{y^2}{36}=1100x2​+36y2​=1

A fixed sum of distances to two fixed points suggests an ellipse. The foci are (±4,0)(\pm4,0)(±4,0), so the centre is the origin and c=4c=4c=4.

2a=10⟹a=5,b2=a2−c2=25−16=9.2a=10\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a=5,\qquad b^2=a^2-c^2=25-16=9.2a=10⟹a=5,b2=a2−c2=25−16=9.

Therefore

x225+y29=1;(b).\boxed{\frac{x^2}{25}+\frac{y^2}{9}=1;\quad\text{(b)}}.25x2​+9y2​=1;(b)​.

Check the existence condition: the sum 10 is greater than the focal separation 8. At (0,3)(0,3)(0,3), both distances are 5; at (5,0)(5,0)(5,0) they are 1 and 9. The same total is obtained in both cases.

Question 10 — A normal stands perpendicular to the tangent at the same point

PDF page 98 | MCQ | Notes: C07

  • (c) 25x+20y=13625x+20y=13625x+20y=136
  • (d) 20x−25y=3520x-25y=3520x−25y=35

A normal means perpendicular to the tangent at this point. First verify that the point belongs to the ellipse:

4225+(9/5)29=1625+925=1.\frac{4^2}{25}+\frac{(9/5)^2}{9} =\frac{16}{25}+\frac9{25}=1.2542​+9(9/5)2​=2516​+259​=1.

y′=−9x25y.y'=-\frac{9x}{25y}.y′=−25y9x​.

At (4,9/5)(4,9/5)(4,9/5), the tangent slope is −4/5-4/5−4/5. Thus the normal slope is 5/45/45/4.

y−95=54(x−4)⟹25x−20y=64;(a).y-\frac95=\frac54(x-4) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{25x-20y=64;\quad\text{(a)}}.y−59​=45​(x−4)⟹25x−20y=64;(a)​.

which has slope 5/45/45/4. This avoids differentiating again once the tangent-normal connection is familiar.

Question 11 — Perpendicular tangents trace the director circle

PDF page 98 | MCQ | Notes: C11

The locus of the point of intersection of perpendicular tangents to the ellipse x29+y24=1\dfrac{x^2}{9}+\dfrac{y^2}{4}=19x2​+4y2​=1 is

  • (a) x2+y2=5x^2+y^2=5x2+y2=5
  • (b) x2+y2=36x^2+y^2=36x2+y2=36
  • (c) x2+y2=25x^2+y^2=25x2+y2=25
  • (d) x2+y2=13x^2+y^2=13x2+y2=13

The moving point is outside the ellipse, where the two tangents meet. This locus is called the director circle. Its radius squared is the sum of the squared semiaxes.

For a2=9,b2=4a^2=9,b^2=4a2=9,b2=4,

x2+y2=9+4=13;(d).\boxed{x^2+y^2=9+4=13;\quad\text{(d)}}.x2+y2=9+4=13;(d)​.

Why that sum appears: for an intersection (h,k)(h,k)(h,k), the finite tangent slopes satisfy

(h2−9)m2−2hkm+(k2−4)=0.(h^2-9)m^2-2hkm+(k^2-4)=0.(h2−9)m2−2hkm+(k2−4)=0.

Perpendicular slopes have product −1-1−1, so k2−4=−(h2−9)k^2-4=-(h^2-9)k2−4=−(h2−9), giving h2+k2=13h^2+k^2=13h2+k2=13.

Check the vertical case: (3,2)(3,2)(3,2) has tangents x=3x=3x=3 and y=2y=2y=2. Their angle is 90∘90^\circ90∘, and 32+22=133^2+2^2=1332+22=13. Thus a slope division must not accidentally remove this valid point.

Question 12 — A chord midpoint is not a tangent point

PDF page 98 | MCQ | Notes: C09

The equation of the chord of the ellipse x24+y2=1\dfrac{x^2}{4}+y^2=14x2​+y2=1 whose midpoint is (1,12)\left(1,\dfrac12\right)(1,21​) is

  • (a) x+2y=2x+2y=2x+2y=2
  • (b) x−2y=0x-2y=0x−2y=0
  • (c) x+4y=3x+4y=3x+4y=3
  • (d) 2x+y=522x+y=\dfrac522x+y=25​

The midpoint is inside the ellipse. Its quadratic value is 1/4+1/4=1/21/4+1/4=1/21/4+1/4=1/2, not 1. So using a tangent-at-point formula would answer the wrong question.

Let the endpoints be

A=(1+u,12+v),B=(1−u,12−v).A=\left(1+u,\frac12+v\right),\qquad B=\left(1-u,\frac12-v\right).A=(1+u,21​+v),B=(1−u,21​−v).

Put both in x2/4+y2=1x^2/4+y^2=1x2/4+y2=1 and subtract:

(1+u)2−(1−u)24+(12+v)2−(12−v)2=0.\frac{(1+u)^2-(1-u)^2}{4} +\left(\frac12+v\right)^2-\left(\frac12-v\right)^2=0.4(1+u)2−(1−u)2​+(21​+v)2−(21​−v)2=0.

This becomes u+2v=0u+2v=0u+2v=0. Thus their joining line through the midpoint obeys

(x−1)+2(y−12)=0.(x-1)+2\left(y-\frac12\right)=0.(x−1)+2(y−21​)=0. x+2y=2;(a).\boxed{x+2y=2;\quad\text{(a)}}.x+2y=2;(a)​.

a2xae−b2yb2/a=a2−b2⟹axe−ay=a2e2.\frac{a^2x}{ae}-\frac{b^2y}{b^2/a}=a^2-b^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{ax}{e}-ay=a^2e^2.aea2x​−b2/ab2y​=a2−b2⟹eax​−ay=a2e2.

Thus

e4+e2=1.e^4+e^2=1.e4+e2=1.

After this chapter

Keep the roles clear: the centre gives symmetry, the foci give the distance sum, a tangent follows the curve, a normal is perpendicular to that tangent, and a midpoint lies halfway along a chord. Rebuild a formula from its picture when recall is uncertain. All alternatives are fully visible for the later booklet.
